The Sage Shushani: A Historical, Existentialist, and Textual Analysis

This source offers a multidimensional analysis of the mysterious figure of "Monsieur Shushani," a phenomenal and wandering genius who profoundly influenced the greatest philosophers of the twentieth century while concealing his biographical identity. The text surveys the historical theses regarding his identity, with emphasis on his identification as Hillel Perlman, a student of Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook, and details his intellectual network of connections with figures such as Elie Wiesel and Emmanuel Levinas. The central portion of the composition is dedicated to his pedagogical and hermeneutic doctrine, termed "the pedagogy of the shard and the pearl," which demands of the student active effort to dive into the depth of textual meaning beyond the revealed words. Finally, the article examines the contents of his personal notebooks, which reveal a rare synthesis between advanced mathematics and physics alongside Kabbalah and radical biblical exegesis, and sketches the portrait of an intellectual who sought absolute intellectual freedom on the margins of society.

The Halakhic Doctrine, Pedagogical Work, and Research Orientations of the Sage Shushani: A Historical, Existentialist, and Textual Analysis

Introduction and Historical Context: The Man Who Became an Enigma

Monsieur Shushani remains one of the most mysterious, fascinating, and influential figures on Jewish and general thought in the twentieth century.[1, 2] He combined inconceivable expertise in all sources of Torah, Talmud, halakhah, and Kabbalah with absolute mastery of exact sciences, modern Western philosophy, classical literature, and at least thirty different languages.[3, 4, 5] Despite his enormous influence on the greatest philosophers and intellectuals of his generation, Shushani chose to live as a homeless wanderer, neglected in his external appearance and devoid of possessions, while zealously concealing the details of his identity and his personal writings.[1, 4, 5]

For decades, intensive efforts were made to decipher the enigma of Shushani's life and identity, with the filmmaker Michael Grinshpan dedicating an entire decade, between 2013 and 2023, to comprehensive journeys of meetings and investigations around the world.[6, 7] This research yielded the documentary film "The Shushani Enigma," which won the award for best documentary film of 2023 and exposed extensive aspects of his life.[7] The historical research and recent discoveries in his handwriting present two central theses regarding his origin and real name.[4, 7] The central thesis, supported by prominent scholars such as Moshe Nachmani and Dr. Yael Levin, identifies him as Rabbi Hillel Perlman, a Lithuanian prodigy and distinguished student of Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook.[3, 4] In contrast, certain archival findings suggest an alternative narrative identifying him as Mordechai Ohana (or Ochanoneh), born in Marrakesh, Morocco.[7]

Comparison of Biographical Identity Hypotheses

Significant physical evidence for the Hillel Perlman thesis was found on the flyleaf of the Ramchal's Kabbalistic book Kelach Pitchei Chokhmah (One Hundred Thirty-Eight Gates of Wisdom) (Warsaw edition), where his explicit signature appears in pencil: "The book belongs to me Hillel Perelman studying at the Pri Etz Chaim yeshivah in Meah Shearim," alongside a rare stamp bearing the inscription "Hillel Perelman Jerusalem."[9] This discovery grants an authentic glimpse into his early days in the Land as a young boy of about 14 and even less, confirming the legends about his genius in Kabbalah already in his childhood, similar to testimony that he knew all of Sifra de-Tzniuta (The Book of Concealment) by heart at age six.[9] An interesting linguistic connection proposed by Rabbi Shimon Shlomo Zilber shows that the name "Hillel Perelman" in full Yiddish spelling yields the gematria value 606, the exact count of the letters shin-vav-shin, and thus the name "Shushani" means "shin-vav-shin-ani" (I am Hillel Perlman).[9]

The historical research uncovers a dramatic and obscure chapter regarding Shushani's studies in his youth at Rabbi Kook's yeshivah in Jaffa, which operated on the upper floor of the Sha'arei Torah workshop building around 1900.[9] This yeshivah, which was characterized by intensive engagement with esoteric Torah and the concealed writings of Rabbi Kook, was intentionally hidden by its graduates, and its historical research is still in its infancy.[8, 9] Recently, the official stamp of the yeshivah was discovered, constituting the only physical remnant of it.[9] During this period, Shushani studied in chavruta (study partnership) with Rabbi Yechiel Michel Kibelwitz (who left moving testimony about Rabbi Kook) and Rabbi Meir Goldberg, alongside other prominent students such as the entrepreneur Asher Rivlin (founder of "Religious Scouts") and Avraham Yosef Hertzfeld.[9] The extensive correspondence between Rabbi Kook and Shushani at the beginning of World War I, alongside Rabbi Kook's letters referring to Perlman by the epithet "the groom" and describing him as "sharp, erudite, complete, and of great wisdom," establish the deep theological and personal connection between them.[4, 9] The history of this institution is extensively documented in the book She'areha Ne'ulim (Her Gates Are Locked).[9]

During various stations of his life, Shushani was hospitalized for a certain period at the "Bikur Cholim" hospital in Jerusalem, and his name was recorded in the institution's book of patients.[9] The journalist David Giladi (grandfather of Yair Lapid) even met him on a ship's deck and published his astonished impressions of his genius and extraordinary personality.[4, 9] The person closest to him in those days is described as Rabbi Menachem Perlman, who knew Shushani and his secrets better than anyone.[9]

The Intellectual Network and Influence on Twentieth-Century Thinkers

Shushani's work as a teacher left an indelible mark on a series of famous thinkers who saw in him a rare teacher who completely changed their lives and thought.[1, 10] He did not perceive himself as creating a closed philosophical system but rather as a pedagogical channel awakening the student to independent, skeptical, and uncompromising thinking.[5, 11]

The Network of Influence and Central Students

Emmanuel Levinas: The renowned French philosopher is considered one of Shushani's most prominent and influenced students.[4, 5] Levinas called him "a wonderful and cruel teacher," and emphasized that Shushani was the one who opened the gates of the Talmud before him and gave him the foundation for his philosophical-ethical readings.[4, 5] Because of his neglected appearance and lack of hygiene, Levinas's wife did not agree that he should teach in their home, and the two conducted their marathon Talmud lessons on the platforms of the Paris metro.[4] From the notebooks it emerges that Shushani engaged extensively in "moral philosophy," an engagement that directly influenced the Levinasian formulation of infinite responsibility to the Other.[5]

Elie Wiesel: The Nobel Peace Prize laureate described Shushani in his autobiography and books as a Kabbalistic and mysterious figure whose age or origin no one knew, and defined him as a wandering Jew who looked like a beggar but held in his mind all the treasures of the human spirit.[4, 5] Wiesel admired his ability to quote by heart from the Indian Vedas alongside the Sefer ha-Zohar (Book of Splendor).[5] After Shushani's death, Wiesel published a moving eulogy in the newspaper Ha-Tzofeh and met with Shushani's nephew to authenticate his identity as Hillel Perlman.[4, 5]

Professor Shalom Rosenberg: One of the senior thinkers in Israel and formerly head of the Department of Jewish Thought at the Hebrew University.[5] Rosenberg studied with Shushani in South America and was at his side in his final moments in Durazno, Uruguay, during a seminar for Bnei Akiva members and religious teachers.[5] Rosenberg is the one who rescued and donated dozens of Shushani's notebooks to the National Library, out of understanding that they constitute the only primary written source he left behind.[5]

Yehuda Leon Ashkenazi (Manitou) and André Neher: Leading thinkers in postwar French Judaism who absorbed from Shushani the methodology of dynamic reading, which dismantles the external verbal structure in order to expose the ideational potential embedded within it.[1, 10]

Professor Zvi Bachrach: The prominent historian and scholar who studied with Shushani during the latter's stay at Kibbutz Be'erot Yitzhak, testimony that attests to the fact that Shushani disseminated his teaching also among young pioneering and religious communities in Israel.[7, 11]

The period of World War II shaped part of the mythical dimensions of his figure as a savior of lives and as one who himself survived in miraculous ways.[7] After his fiancée Sarah Abitbol was mur
Faced with death before his eyes in Paris at the hands of the Germans, Shoshani fled to Switzerland.[4, 7] In order not to be extradited back into Nazi hands, he feigned insanity and was diagnosed with psychopathic neurosis.[7] His most famous encounter with the Gestapo occurred when he was arrested on suspicion of being a Jew.[7] Shoshani insisted that he was Muslim, and to verify his claim the Germans brought the imam of Paris to examine him.[7] According to the testimony of Dr. Michel Goldberg, after a two-hour in-depth theological and philosophical conversation on the Quran, the imam emerged moved and declared to the Nazi officer that the man was a devout Muslim, adding that he had never learned about Islam as he had learned from Shoshani's mouth in those two hours.[7]

His Pedagogical and Theoretical System: The Pedagogy of the Potsherd and the Pearl and the Renewed PaRDeS

Shoshani's Torah system was not formulated in systematic articles but rather in living encounter and in an uncompromising hermeneutic methodology.[5, 11] Understanding the hidden and the secret for him does not pass through mystical experiences, ecstasy, or abandonment of reason, but precisely through the paths of understanding, wisdom, and the intellectual capacity of deconstruction and reconstruction.[11]

The Pedagogy of the Potsherd and the Pearl

Within his commentary on the opening of parashat Toldot, Shoshani analyzes the Talmudic aggadah about the debate between Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba, in which Rabbi Yoḥanan said: "Had I not lifted the potsherd for you, you would not have found the pearl beneath it."[11] From this story Shoshani formulated a system of seven strict pedagogical laws defining the proper dynamic between teacher and student.[11]

According to this conception, the teacher's role is limited solely to removing the external obstacle—the potsherd covering the truth—and he is absolutely forbidden to point directly to the pearl itself.[11] The student is required to be an active diver, who understands by his own powers how to lift the potsherd, dive to the depths, and discover the profound meaning.[11] Independent discovery is the sole condition for understanding the true value of understanding.[11] Even when the student errs during learning and lifts up a simple potsherd with the mistaken thought that it is a pearl, the teacher is forbidden to provide him with the correct answer.[11] The teacher's role remains to continue removing the intellectual potsherds surrounding him, to guide him to determine what is correct, and to enable him to reach the true pearl himself.[11] From this emerges Shoshani's demand of his students not to remain with the potsherd—that is, with the external charm of stories and aggadot—but to dive into the words themselves, to turn them over, to examine them carefully, and to discover what lies beyond them.[11]

The Four Levels of PaRDeS in Ḥakham Shoshani's Interpretation

Shoshani's hermeneutics proposes a renewed structural definition of the four levels of PaRDeS, shifting the weight from the conventional definitions to a sophisticated philosophical process of decoding and determination for the reader.[11]

The search for the hidden in Shoshani does not deviate from language but occurs within it.[11] His method of study passes through meticulous deconstruction of words and discovery of the infinite space of meanings within them.[11] In coming to interpret the verse in Proverbs (1:28): "Then shall they call upon me, but I will not answer; they shall seek me early, but they shall not find me," Shoshani explains that the students will search for the letter nun (נ) and will not find it.[12] This interpretation alludes to his method whereby the simple precedes the complex in spiritual rank, just as the wise man precedes the fool, good precedes evil, and the whole precedes the defective.[12] Logic for Shoshani is essentially precision and order, based on sharp distinction between secondary and primary, and between complicated and simple.[12] Shoshani saw the entire world as a collection of texts to be interpreted again and again, and held the position that in every single verse there are two million four hundred thousand possible interpretations.[7]

The Textual Structure and Spatial Codes of the Notebooks

The personal notebooks that Shoshani left behind serve as material evidence of his unique method of study and writing.[1, 5] These are extremely difficult texts to decode, in which the hidden exceeds the revealed.[5] The writing is dense, lacking connecting words and full of allusions and acronyms only, which greatly complicates the connection and continuous understanding of the ideas.[1, 11] Shoshani was accustomed to emphasizing certain parts of quotations, omitting other parts, or joining together completely different sources.[1] Many sources, and especially biblical verses, are not brought in their language but through numerical reference to their precise location or short keywords.[1]

The spatial organization of the pages is sophisticated and dynamic.[1] Although most lines are written horizontally, Shoshani incorporated notes and supplements written vertically, and divided the pages into separate units by means of dividing lines and large spaces, apparently intended to allow later completion of the material.[1] In several of the notebooks he deliberately skipped entire pages in order to leave room for future expansion of the subject.[1]

For the purpose of shortening his writing method and intellectual encryption, Shoshani borrowed distinct graphic symbols from the world of logic and mathematics, which appear throughout all his paragraphs.[1]

The System of Graphic Symbols in Shoshani's Notebooks

Attempts to decode the notebooks encountered enormous difficulties over the years, and only in recent years, following the archive's donation to the National Library, have researchers and scholars begun to decode them systematically.[1, 5] Michael Grynszpan, in the framework of his work on his film, utilized advanced computer analyses and experts such as Rabbi Uri Sharki, Elimelekh Huna, and Akiva Kahana, in order to break through the veil of encryption and expose parts of the sources of Shoshani's life and thought.[7]

Close Reading in the Decoded Notebooks: Multidisciplinary Investigation

Careful study of the decoded notebooks presents a phenomenal integration between fields of knowledge considered contradictory in classical Western thought, but which coalesce in Shoshani into one harmonic system.[1, 11]

Notebook 1CH1: The Encounter between Mathematics, Physics, and Biology

This notebook (physically marked with the number 2 on its cover) is written in Hebrew and Spanish and contains 60 pages, of which 46 are written and the rest blank.[1] It includes complex mathematical calculations whose context is apparently physical, alongside various lists and a separate page containing logical riddles in Spanish.[1]

In the mathematical domain, surfers and researchers identified in the notebook solutions to systems of algebraic equations, polynomials, hyperbolic functions, use of permutations, and presentation of Pascal's triangle.[1] On page 22 appears an expression representing the Fourier series of a triangular wave:

cos(x) + cos(3x)/3² + cos(5x)/5²

with notation of a small calculation error by Shoshani in defining the denominators.[1] On page 23 appears treatment of complex numbers of the form a+ib, finding the angle by means of:

t = arctan(b/a)

calculation of the distance from the origin defined in the notebook as R = √(a² + b²), and its polar representation as R(cos(t) + i sin(t)).[1] Shoshani discusses group theory, mentions the Persian mathematician al-Khwārizmī (inventor of the algorithm), presents historical formulas such as Faulhaber's formula, and compiles lists of mathematicians with the years of their discoveries.[1] Additionally, there appears advanced use of logarithm tables for performing rapid calculations, while defining complex operational keys.[1]

In the biological domain, pages 17 and 18 contain detailed summaries on cell biology, genetics, and molecular biology.[1] Among other things it is written there: "In each cell 48 chromosomes"—data that corresponds scientifically to apes (whereas in humans there are 46 chromosomes).[1] The page of riddles in Spanish attached to the notebook deals with classic logical problems of truth and falsehood based on liars and truth-tellers with black and blue eyes, alongside mention of the problem of the seven bridges of Königsberg.[1]

Notebook 1CH3: Biblical Hermeneutics, Cosmology, and Kabbalistic Theology

attention to verses and sections from Scripture, and integrates tables constituting complex calendar calculations.[1] The notebook opens with an analysis of Deuteronomy (chapter 18, verses 6-8) dealing with the laws of the Levites.[1] Shoshani focuses on the word "your gates," and interprets the words "where he sojourns" as a halakhic determination that "he has no right to rent."[1] The words "whom the Lord shall choose" he interprets as a process carried out "by a prophet with the agreement of all the tribes," and explains that Scripture left the location of the Temple unspecified because there is no practical legal difference which place the tribes choose—wherever they choose by national consensus, there the Divine Presence will dwell.[1] The expression "like all his brethren the Levites who stand there" Shoshani interprets as establishing the principle of social equality, preventing jealousy on the part of the veteran Levites toward the new Levite who has just come to serve in the Temple.[1]

On page 2a Shoshani develops the governmental and spiritual structure of Israel through the acronym M-SH-K-N, and notes that there is appointment for a judge but no personal appointment to serve in the Temple.[1]

## The Structure of Public Leadership in the M-SH-K-N Model

Shoshani analyzes the concept of self-sacrifice and proposes that the only true signs of love for God are sacrifice.[1] While the sacrifice of property is difficult only for misers, the sacrifice of life itself is the depth of the love of "and you shall live by them"—the realization of a portion of God above in all efforts, without retreating even in situations of danger.[1] The Binding of Isaac was intended "to cleanse" the flaws of idolatry of Terah, Abraham's father.[1]

In the discussion of the death of Nadab and Abihu, Shoshani explains that performing an act without command constitutes a grave sin.[1] Phinehas, in his zealous act, acted on his own because Moses forgot the halakha, and his act is considered a halakha equivalent in value to a command.[1] In this act Phinehas corrected the sin of Aaron's compromise with the Golden Calf (which caused the idolatry of the mixed multitude) and the sin of Nadab and Abihu.[1] Shoshani presents a kabbalistic hint based on acronyms: **N**adab **A**bihu ≡ **N**avi (prophet) **E**liyahu, which confirms the tradition that Phinehas is Elijah.[1]

On page 10b Shoshani proposes a stunning modern cosmological interpretation of the verse "and there was evening and there was morning, one day" (Genesis 1:5), and writes: "Every moment was evening and morning in opposite places," a reference that expresses a clear scientific understanding of the global shape of the earth and geographical time differences.[1] On page 10a he compares Genesis 1:3 to Genesis 1:7, writes the letters gimel and zayin in cursive script and notes that "one sees clearly that their forms are inverted relative to each other" as opposite reflections.[1] He defines night as the time of absence of light (representing death, blindness and foolishness), evening from the language "things will be mixed and not recognized," and morning from the language "and everything will be examined in its light" (the ability to distinguish and examine between things in daylight).[1]

## Notebook 60: "The Oven of Akhnai" and the Ethics of the House of Study

This notebook opens with a linguistic clarification of the phrase "the oven of Akhnai," and proceeds to an in-depth discussion of teacher-student relations and the boundaries of morality.[5] Shoshani asks difficult philosophical-moral questions: Why did Rabbi Yehoshua remain silent twice at the miracles of the carob tree and the stream of water, and intervene only when the walls of the house of study inclined to fall? [5] Shoshani explains this through an analysis of "increasing loss" [5]:

In the miracle of the carob tree's movement there is no real loss to society, and therefore there is no need to dispute the miracle.

In the stream of water flowing backward there is a certain loss, since the water no longer irrigates the fields, but the damage is still bearable.

In the collapse of the house of study there is enormous loss and total destruction of the institution of Torah and society.

Shoshani establishes an axiological determination that the house of study as an institution is eternal as opposed to the temporal and transient human being.[5] Therefore, the walls reached a compromise—they inclined to fall out of respect for Rabbi Yehoshua but did not fall out of respect for Rabbi Eliezer, in order to express the structural need to listen to both sides in a dispute.[5]

Another topic that deeply engaged Shoshani in his writings is the verse in Psalms (89:39): "But You have spurned and rejected; You have been enraged at Your anointed."[7] He wondered why the sages of the assemblies did not omit this difficult verse from the Book of Psalms, and wrote in his notebooks sentences such as "a person is not seized for his anguish," "here despairs 39" and also "God breaks the covenant," which express his deep existential struggle with questions of destruction, divine concealment and the fragility of the historical covenant.[7]

## Summary and Conclusions

The sage Shoshani represents a revolutionary model of a classical scholar and modern intellectual, who refused to accept upon himself the social conventions of the world of academia or the rabbinate, and chose to live on the margins of society in order to preserve his absolute intellectual freedom.[1, 3, 7] His Torah work did not consist of writing systematic books, but rather in producing students who became leading figures in the philosophical and Jewish thought of the twentieth century.[1, 10]

His pedagogical teaching, as emerges from the laws of "The Shard and the Pearl," places a radical demand upon the student: breaking the external verbal barriers, independent thought without compromise and diving beyond words, to the place where wisdom and science merge into a single theological unity.[1, 11] The decipherment of his notebooks, now in progress, continues to reveal the logical, mathematical and kabbalistic depth of the mysterious genius, and promises to continue enriching our understanding regarding the spaces of interpretation and Jewish thought in coming generations.[5, 7, 11]
